newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek premier to discuss military pact with Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Greek premier to discuss military pact with Cyprus.

text.p: Greece and Cyprus will seek to strengthen their joint defence agreement, aimed at deterring a perceived threat from neighbouring Turkey, when their leaders meet this week, Greek officials said on Monday.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis chose Cyprus for his first visit since winning a general election this month to stress the importance his administration attaches to the Mediterranean island, the officials said.

"The Cyprus struggle is a struggle of our nation as a whole. For our government, Cyprus is the top foreign policy issue," he said in a newspaper interview distributed by his office ahead of the visit, which is due to begin on Tuesday.
Underscoring the dangers that lurk in the 22-year Cyprus problem, he added: "Any attempt by the Turkish occupation forces to advance will constitute a cause of war between Greece and Turkey."

In recent months both Athens and Ankara have warned of the dangers of war in the Eastern Mediterranean or over the Aegean Sea, ringing alarm bells in Washington and at the Brussels headquarters of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union. Both countries are NATO members and Greece is a member of the EU.
Greece and Turkey almost clashed militarily in January in a dispute over an uninhabited island, and Cyprus was the scene of several bloody incidents between Greek and Turkish Cypriots in the summer.

Turkey invaded the independent island in 1974 and seized the northern third, where some 30,000 Turkish troops are stationed. The move was in response to a coup attempt by Greek Cypriots, backed by a military junta then ruling in Athens.

The Simitis government is warily eyeing plans for a new U.S. initiative on troubled Greek-Turkish relations and Cyprus. The U.S. push is expected to pick up pace after the U.S. presidential and congressional elections on November 5.

Washington stated its concern over regional tensions and intention to take a more active role in a note to Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos after the socialists won this month's general election.
Greece is concerned that Washington would try to combine all disputes with Turkey into a global negotiation, much like the U.S.-sponsored Dayton meeting to hammer out a Bosnia accord.
Disputes range from a Moslem minority, including ethnic Turks, in northern Greece, and mineral rights in the Aegean to sovereignty over islands and the division of Cyprus.

Simitis and Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides are expected to discuss a common front to any American initiative, and how to face what is likely to be a concerted U.S. effort to resolve at least some Greek-Turkish problems.
Simitis is during his visit due to meet Clerides and attend an all-party national council and a military parade commemorating Cyprus's independence from British rule in 1960.
Greece and Cyprus signed a joint military agreement in 1993 which, in effect, stretches Athens' defence lines to include the island and seeks to ensure compatibility between the two forces.

Compatibility covers strategy, equipment and problems such as Cyprus's inability to service Greece's U.S.-built F-16 fighters fully. The defence pact is expected to figure large in the talks, with Athens seeking to strengthen it and find practical ways to implement it.
